title: Macroscopic wall pressure and microscopic contact load in crowds without egress: social-group cohesion and boundary buffering
abstract: Crowd safety in confined venues is usually evaluated through evacuation performance or pre-collision avoidance, while direct mechanical hazards in dense gatherings without egress remain poorly understood. We study an Elastic Reorientation Model (ERM), a Social Force Model (SFM), and their coupled dynamics. Post-collision behavior is represented by social-group cohesion ($γ_g$) and wall buffering ($γ_w$), while risk is quantified by the macroscopic wall line pressure ($P_{\text{wall}}$) and the microscopic maximum per-agent collision impulse ($δp_{\text{max}}$). In the ERM, cohesion and wall buffering generally reduce $P_{\text{wall}}$ by retaining agents in the bulk, but large groups exhibit a high-$δp_{\text{max}}$ hazard window at intermediate cohesion. As $γ_g\rightarrow1$, local pairing suppresses cluster growth and shifts kinetic energy from relative to center-of-mass motion, reducing $δp_{\text{max}}$. SFM pushing and sliding amplify $δp_{\text{max}}$, especially when agent-agent and agent-wall interactions coexist, while active driving raises $P_{\text{wall}}$ through near-wall accumulation. The coupled dynamics produces a wall-pressure/contact-load ($P$-$p$) trade-off. Finite-size scaling reveals an independent-agent-induced phase boundary at $γ_w=0.5$, characterized by a susceptibility discontinuity, and a grouped-agent-induced continuous phase boundary along a finite segment of $(1-γ_w)(1-γ_g)=0.5$, characterized by divergent susceptibility and terminating at a critical point. Both disappear in the social-force-free ERM, showing that they emerge from the coupled ERM+SFM dynamics. These results provide mechanistic guidance for crowd-risk mitigation and safety planning in high-density venues without egress.
summary: This work models mechanical safety risks in extremely dense crowds trapped without escape routes. By coupling elastic collision dynamics with social forces, the authors quantify trade-offs between overall wall pressure and peak collision loads. The findings provide mechanistic insights into how social behaviors like cohesion and buffering dictate crowd risk profiles.
main_problem: The study investigates direct mechanical hazards in dense, confined crowds that lack any means of egress, moving beyond typical evacuation safety metrics.
main_result: The paper establishes a critical wall-pressure/contact-load trade-off and identifies distinct phase boundaries (independent vs. grouped agents) emerging only from the coupled dynamics of elastic reorientation and social forces.
method: The authors employ multi-scale modeling, combining an Elastic Reorientation Model (ERM) with a Social Force Model (SFM) to simulate agent interactions under high density.
model_or_system: The system models N agents as rigid disks in a 2D confined domain. Interactions are governed by collision-triggered dynamics (conserving kinetic energy) and persistent social forces, incorporating parameters for group cohesion ($\gamma_g$) and wall buffering ($\gamma_w$).
key_observables: Macroscopic wall line pressure ($P_{	ext{wall}}$), microscopic maximum per-agent collision impulse ($\delta p_{\max}$), and susceptibility measures used to locate phase boundaries.
important_parameters: Cohesion strength ($\gamma_g$), wall buffering strength ($\gamma_w$), and the relative influence of SFM forces (pushing/sliding) versus purely elastic collisions.
main_assumptions: The rigid disk approximation is used, neglecting body deformation; safety criteria are defined by comparing $\delta p_{\max}$ to a critical impulse $p^*$.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the schematic of the system domain and show how different initial condition distributions yield similar final state dynamics for the baseline elastic collision model.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first defining the mechanical hazards, then detailing the coupled ERM+SFM framework, analyzing the resulting trade-offs ($P$-$p$), and finally using finite-size scaling to map out distinct phase boundaries associated with agent grouping and boundary effects.
why_interesting: While focused on classical physics, the analysis of emergent collective behavior, phase transitions (susceptibility discontinuities), and non-equilibrium steady states in a highly interacting many-body system shares conceptual overlap with critical phenomena studied in statistical mechanics.
